The correct exponent is α = 1/2, which matches Solution 1.

**Why the first chaos drops out.** For Berry's random wave model the spectral measure is uniform on the unit sphere. The first-chaos part of the excursion volume, integrated against a test function rescaled to a large scale R, has variance governed by \(\hat\varphi_R(\xi)=R^d\hat\varphi(R\xi)\) evaluated on \(|\xi|=1\). This decays rapidly in R, so the first chaos is negligible at large scales.

**Why the second chaos dominates.** For u > 0 the second-chaos coefficient is nonzero. It is proportional to \(uφ(u)/2\), where φ is the standard Gaussian density. Its covariance is proportional to \(K(r)^2\). Since \(K(r)\sim C\,r^{-(d-1)/2}\cos(r+\text{phase})\), the non-oscillatory part of \(K^2\) decays like \(r^{-(d-1)}\).

**Spectral density.** The Fourier transform of \(|x|^{-(d-1)}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is proportional to \(|\xi|^{-d+(d-1)}=|\xi|^{-1}\). The field \((-\Delta)^{-\alpha}W\) has spectral density \(|\xi|^{-2\alpha}\). Matching exponents gives \(2\alpha=1\), so \(\alpha=1/2\).

**Checking the other solutions.**
- Solution 2 uses a kernel \(|x-y|^{-(d-1)/2}\), which is the decay of K itself rather than of K². This gives the wrong exponent.
- Solution 3 uses the first chaos and a heuristic spectral density \(|\xi|^{-(d-1)}\). The first chaos does not survive at large scales, so this is wrong as well.

CHOICE: 1
